analysis.one_liner: Restores federal protections for renters living in homes lost to foreclosure.
analysis.headline: The Senate bill restoring renter protections after foreclosure never got a hearing or a vote; it died in committee when the 2017-2018 Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: A 2009 law gave renters living in foreclosed homes the right to stay: new owners had to give them 90 days' notice before eviction, and tenants with leases could stay until the lease ended, including families using housing vouchers. That law expired at the end of 2014. This bill would have brought those protections back permanently by repealing the expiration date.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters in homes that get foreclosed — including month-to-month tenants, families with fixed-term leases, and households using Section 8 housing vouchers — who would keep at least 90 days to find a new place instead of being removed when the new owner takes over.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the 2014 expiration clause of the Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act of 2009 and restores its tenant protections as if the law had never lapsed.

Under the restored law, a buyer of a foreclosed home could not evict a tenant immediately: tenants on month-to-month leases get 90 days' notice, and tenants with fixed-term leases get to stay through the lease term, with Section 8 voucher holders protected through the full lease term.
The protections would be permanent rather than temporary, so renters would not lose them again to an expiration date.

analysis.who_pays: Banks that foreclose and investors who buy foreclosed homes, who would have to keep the current tenant in place for the notice or lease period rather than take the property vacant. Buyers of foreclosed properties would also face a smaller pool of vacant units to flip or re-rent.

drawbacks.text: Buyers of foreclosed homes would lose the ability to take a property vacant immediately after closing; under the bill, a 90-day notice or an existing lease would control how long a tenant could stay.

The extra holding period can be a real cost to small landlords and buyers who purchase foreclosed homes to renovate and re-rent, and some argue it makes foreclosed properties less attractive purchases; the counterargument is that it is a modest wait compared with the family losing its home with no notice.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is substantial: foreclosure typically forces the homeowner out, and before this law it also forced out renters who paid their rent and did nothing wrong. The cost falls on the new owner as a 90-day notice or an existing lease term — a real but bounded inconvenience. The main design question is whether protections should cover all tenants or only voucher holders and longer leases; this bill chose broad coverage, which favors tenants over the convenience of foreclosure buyers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, and that is where it stayed — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Blumenthal introduced the bill on February 7, 2017, joined by six Democratic cosponsors.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs on the day it was introduced.
No further action is recorded: the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and expired with the 115th Congress in January 2019.
The protections it would have restored remain lapsed unless Congress acts; a nearly identical one-chamber effort (H.R. 3548) also did not advance in this Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks that foreclose on homes and investors who buy them came out ahead, keeping the freedom to remove tenants immediately after foreclosure. Renters living in foreclosed homes continued to face eviction with little or no notice, since the 2014 expiration was never undone in this Congress.

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to permanently restore the Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act of 2009.

for.name: Sens. Stabenow, Menendez, Whitehouse, and Franken
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, bringing total support to seven senators, all Democrats.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Sen. Mike Crapo, R-ID)
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote — leaving it to expire.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled floor time for the bill, which had not cleared committee.

sides.party_line_note: All seven supporters were Democrats; no Republican senator signed on, and the bill's committee of referral had a Republican chairman and majority during the 115th Congress.

industries.industry: Banks and mortgage servicers that foreclose
industries.note: The bill would have required a new owner after foreclosure to give tenants at least 90 days' notice or honor the existing lease instead of taking the home vacant. Its defeat lets banks continue selling foreclosed homes with tenants still in them.

Foreclosure buyers would have had to wait out a notice period or a lease before renovating or re-renting. Because the bill died, they can still acquire these homes on the expectation of quick possession, which comes at the expense of the tenants living there.
